explainers.title: Hello again, and welcome to Analysis
explainers.body:
Hello, and welcome back to Global Perspectives at Ehel Academy. In Unit 1 you grew your first thinking skill, Research. You learned to ask good questions, find things out from books and people, and keep a tidy record. That was a wonderful start. Now you are ready for the next skill.

Remember that this subject grows six thinking skills. You build them one at a time, and each one helps the others:

This whole unit is about the second skill: Analysis. Research helped you find out what is happening. Analysis asks the deeper questions: why does it happen, who sees it differently, and what could we do about it? It is a skill you already use a little every day.
bullets: Research - finding out about the world in a careful way.
Analysis - looking closely at a topic and asking why things happen.
Evaluation - deciding how good an idea or a fact really is.
Reflection - thinking about how you learn.
Collaboration - working well with other people.
Communication - sharing your ideas so others understand.

explainers.title: How you will learn this unit
explainers.body:
You learn in the Ehel Academy way. Three kinds of help work together:

Analysis grows fastest when you talk, because it is all about seeing a topic from more than one side. In the old way of this subject, children were told to 'talk to a partner' or 'talk as a class'. In our way, your AI tutor is your partner and your class. So every time you see an 'Ask Your AI Tutor' box, have a real chat with it, and ask it what someone who thinks differently might say.

Your analysis skills will grow in three steps this year, like a young tree growing taller. First you are starting a skill. Then you are developing it. Then you are getting better at it. Do not worry if something feels tricky at first. Starting is meant to feel like a first try.
bullets: You, at your own speed. You read, think and do the activities in your own time. You can go slowly on a hard idea, or quickly on an easy one.

Your AI tutor, ready any time, day or night. When this book says 'Ask Your AI Tutor', you talk to your tutor like a friendly helper. It will chat about your ideas, ask you kind questions back, and help you at any hour.
Your teacher, about twice a week. In your live sessions you share your best thinking and ask your biggest questions.

explainers.title: Meet Rami, our analyst for this unit
explainers.body:
To make each idea clear, we will follow one Year 4 learner all the way through. His name is Rami, and he is a pupil at Ehel Academy in Hargeisa.

One afternoon, Rami is eating a piece of chocolate. He loves it. Then he stops and wonders: where does chocolate actually come from, who makes it, and is everyone treated fairly along the way? He does not know the answer yet. But that little wonder is the start of some real analysis.

That question becomes Rami's project for this unit. Notice that Rami is not only finding out about chocolate, as he would in Research. He is looking closely: who grows it, who gets paid, and how different people feel about it. As you meet each new analysis skill, you will see what Rami does with it, and you will do the very same thing with a topic that matters to you.

explainers.title: Your Challenge: the project that runs through the unit
explainers.body:
Just like in Research, this unit builds one big project we call your Challenge. A Challenge is a real topic that matters where you live and also in the wider world. You come back to it, lesson after lesson, and each new analysis skill adds another piece.

Rami's Challenge is how and where chocolate is made, and whether it is fair. You can pick the same topic, or choose your own. The best topic for Analysis is one where people honestly think different things. Here are some good Challenge topics for Year 4:

Your classmates will care about different things. Layla wants to save the town park. Idris wonders why some streets have no vegetable shop. Nadia thinks a lot about being fair. Any of these could grow into a strong Challenge.

You do not have to choose right now. As you work, keep a note of any topic that makes you curious, especially one where people would not all agree.
bullets: How and where chocolate is made, and whether the farmers are paid fairly
The goods our own region sells to the world, like bananas, sesame and frankincense
A local green space, like a town park, and who it is for
Fresh fruit and vegetables, and whether every family can reach them
Litter, or keeping our neighbourhood clean and pleasant
Internet for homework, and whether every child can get online

explainers.title: So what is analysis?
explainers.body:
The word analysis means looking closely at something to understand the parts inside it. When you analyse a topic, you stop treating it as one big lump and start asking careful questions about the pieces. A simple way to remember it is this: research gathers the pieces, and analysis works out how the pieces fit together.

Good analysis uses four kinds of thinking, and this unit teaches all four:

That is the whole unit in four ideas: perspectives, data, actions, and a positive action. Keep those four words in mind and analysis will feel simple.
bullets: Seeing perspectives - the different ways people think about a topic, and their reasons.
Reading data - what the numbers in a chart, table or graph really show.
Thinking about actions - why people do things, and how their actions affect other people.
Choosing a positive action - deciding what you could do to make a real difference to a local topic.

explainers.title: Rami looks closely at chocolate
explainers.body: Let us follow Rami's first look at his Challenge. It shows all four parts of analysis working together.

explainers.title: Starting to analyse
explainers.body: You will begin with the first three analysis skills. At the Starting stage, you learn to say what one person thinks and why, to read what data shows, and to think of a first action for a local topic. Take these gently. Starting is meant to feel like a first try.

explainers.title: Starting skill 1: Say what a person thinks, and why
explainers.body:
The first skill in Analysis is the perspective. A perspective is a way of seeing a topic, a point of view. On almost any topic, people honestly think different things, and each person has their own reasons. A good analyst does not just say 'she is right' or 'he is wrong' straight away. First they try to see the topic through each person's eyes.

The most important part of a perspective is the reason. Saying 'I think it was unfair' is a start. Saying 'I think it was unfair because they did not have the same chance' is a real perspective. The little word 'because' turns an opinion into good analysis.

Here you also meet two words that sound alike but are different: equal and fair. Equal means everyone gets exactly the same. Fair means everyone gets what they need to have a fair chance. They are not always the same thing, as Rami's class found out.

explainers.title: Starting skill 2: Say what the data shows
explainers.body:
Not all information is words. Some of the strongest information is data: numbers and counts, often shown in a chart, a table or a graph. You may already know some ways to show data: a tally chart for counting, a bar graph for comparing, a Venn diagram for sorting, and a line graph for change over time. A good analyst can look at data and say clearly what it shows.

When you meet data, read it calmly and in order. First the title (what is it about?). Then the labels (what is being counted?). Then the numbers (which is the biggest, which is the smallest?). After that, you can check something important: does the data actually back up what someone said?

explainers.title: Starting skill 3: My reasons, and a first idea to help
explainers.body:
Analysis is not only about looking. It is also about doing. Every day, you take actions that affect other people, and each action has a reason. A good analyst can say what they did, and why, and how it helped someone.

You help in more places than you might think: in your home, in your neighbourhood, and sometimes for a wider community far away. Naming your own reasons is good practice for understanding why other people act, too.

For any local topic, a starting analyst asks two questions: what exactly is the problem, and what is one thing I could do to help? You do not need a huge plan yet. One good idea is a fine place to start.
bullets: The town park needs a tidy-up, and could be used more.
Not every child has the internet, so homework is harder for some.
Some families cannot easily reach fresh fruit and vegetables.
There is no computer club for children who would love one.
The community garden needs helping hands.

explainers.title: Developing your analysis
explainers.body: Now you take each skill a step further. At the Developing stage, you notice that many people, not just one, think different things. You learn to hunt for the exact data that answers a question. And you think harder about how your actions affect others, and about planning a real action.

explainers.title: Developing skill 1: Different people think different things
explainers.body:
At the Starting stage you described what one person thinks. Now you notice something bigger: on most topics there is not just one perspective, there are several. A strong analyst collects a whole range of perspectives before making up their mind.

Think of the chocolate again. It is one topic, but listen to how many different people see it:

None of these people is silly or wrong. Each one sees the topic from where they stand. Noticing that many honest people think many different things, and that each has a reason, is the heart of Global Perspectives.
bullets: A cocoa farmer far away: I work hard in the heat, but I am paid very little for my beans.
A child who eats chocolate: I love the taste, and I never thought about who grew it.
A shopkeeper: fair-trade chocolate costs a little more, and I am not sure people will buy it.
A parent buying chocolate: I want a fair price for the farmer, but I also count my money carefully.

explainers.title: Developing skill 2: Find the useful data to answer a question
explainers.body:
At the Starting stage you said what data shows. Now you learn to hunt in the data for the exact part that answers your question. Sometimes data comes in a table, and sometimes on a map. A good analyst knows where to look, and can check whether a claim is really true.

Rami's class studied a town where the fresh fruit and vegetable shops were not spread out evenly. They had a table showing, for each district, how many fresh-food shops there were, how many older people lived there, and how many families were poor.

explainers.title: Developing skill 3: How my actions affect others, and planning an action
explainers.body:
Now you think harder about actions. Every action you take has a reason, and it also has an effect on other people. A careful analyst thinks about both before acting. To do this well, it helps to plan an action, instead of just rushing in.

A good plan answers a few clear questions: Where will I do it? What will I do? Why? What have I found out first? How will it affect other people? How will it affect me? And what difference will it make?

explainers.title: Getting better at analysis
explainers.body: This is the deepest stage. Now you do not just say that people think differently, you explain why. You use data to reach a conclusion. And you weigh several actions to choose the one that would work best.

explainers.title: Getting better skill 1: Explain why people think differently
explainers.body:
At the Developing stage you noticed that people think different things. Now you ask the deeper question: why? People's perspectives are shaped by their age, where they live, what they enjoy, and what they need. When you can explain the reason behind a view, you truly understand it.

Rami's class looked at a topic close to home: their beloved Green Park. The town wanted to add a new water-play fountain, but to pay for it the entrance fee would go up. Should a town park be free for everyone? People felt very differently, and each had a reason.

explainers.title: Getting better skill 2: Use data to reach a simple conclusion
explainers.body:
Now you use data to reach a conclusion. A conclusion is a careful sentence that sums up what the data tells you, and often why. To do this well, you read the numbers and then link them to what was happening at the time.

Rami's class had a table of how many visitors came to the Green Park each week, month by month. They also had some notes: the fee went up on the first of May, and the new water-play fountain opened at the end of July. Hot months make the middle of the day very warm.

explainers.title: Getting better skill 3: Why people act, and choosing the best action
explainers.body:
The last skill brings everything together. You think about why other people act the way they do, how their actions affect others, and then you choose the most effective action, which means the one that would work best.

One day a sad headline appeared: the Green Park might close, because it costs the town a lot of money each year. Rami noticed that people reacted very differently, because the park affected them in different ways.

explainers.title: How analysis helps the other five skills
explainers.body:
Analysis sits in the middle of the six skills, and it connects to every one of them.

So the thinking you practise here is never wasted. Analysis is the bridge between simply knowing about a topic and being able to judge it, talk about it, and act on it wisely.
bullets: Research feeds analysis: you must gather information before you can look closely at why things happen.
Evaluation grows from analysis: once you can see the different views, you can decide which idea is strongest.
Reflection grows every time you notice how your analysis changed your mind.
Collaboration gets better when you can understand other people's perspectives, not only your own.
Communication is clearer and fairer when it rests on careful analysis instead of a first reaction.

explainers.title: Putting it all together
explainers.body: You have now met every analysis skill in this unit. Here is the whole journey in simple steps you can use for any topic:
bullets: See the different perspectives, and ask for each person's reason.
Read the data in a chart or table, and check whether it backs up a claim.
Think about actions: why people do things, and how their actions affect others.
Choose a positive action, and pick the one that would be most effective.

explainers.title: What comes next
explainers.body: The next unit is Evaluation. Once you can analyse a topic, evaluation teaches you to weigh ideas and evidence and decide how strong each one really is. Strong analysis now will make strong evaluation much easier later. Well done for taking your thinking to a new level in Global Perspectives.

bigIdeas.title: One big idea to remember
lines: In Global Perspectives, the topic is like a bus, and the skill is where the bus takes you.
We will use real topics, like chocolate, a town park, and fresh food.
But the real prize is to become a clear thinker who can look closely at almost any topic and see it from many sides.

bigIdeas.title: A perspective needs a reason
lines: A weak perspective just says: I think it was unfair.
A strong perspective says: I think it was unfair, because everyone did not have the same chance.
When someone tells you what they think, a kind analyst asks: why do you think that? What is your reason?

bigIdeas.title: Look for more than one perspective
lines: A weak analyst describes only their own view.
A strong analyst asks: who else has a stake in this, and what would they say?
Try to find at least three perspectives on your topic before you decide what you think.

bigIdeas.title: The four parts of analysis
lines: Whenever you feel stuck, come back to these four words.
Perspectives: the different ways people think, and their reasons.
Data: what the numbers in a chart or table really show.
Actions: why people do things, and how their actions affect others.
Positive action: the best thing you could do to help.

bigIdeas.title: Sentence starters for a perspective
lines: ... thinks that ...
This is because ...
They feel ... about it.
Another person might think ... because ...

bigIdeas.title: Kinds of data display you might see
lines: Tally chart: quick marks for counting things.
Bar graph: bars of different heights, to compare amounts.
Venn diagram: circles that overlap, to sort things into groups.
Line graph or table: to show how something changes over time.

bigIdeas.title: Little words that point to causes and effects
lines: Cause words: because, since, the reason is.
Consequence words: so, then, as a result, this leads to.
When you read, look for these words. They point straight to the reasons and the results.

bigIdeas.title: Your Challenge runs through everything
lines: Pick one real topic to analyse across this whole unit. This is your Challenge.
You may use chocolate and fair trade, like Rami, or pick a local topic where people think different things.
You will build on it in every activity, so choose something you really care about.

bigIdeas.title: Sentence starters and word bank
lines: Sentence starters: ... thinks the competition was ... This is because ... He feels ...
Word bank: happy, upset, fair, unfair, equal, unequal, deserved, did not deserve, materials, chance.
Every perspective needs the word because, followed by a reason.

models.title: Analysis happens in everyday life too
lines: Imagine two friends both want to play at break. One wants football. One wants to sit and draw.
Research would ask: what does each friend want to do?
Analysis goes further. It asks why: maybe one loves running, and the other hurt their foot.
It thinks about actions too: if they only play football, is that fair to the friend who cannot run today?
Working all of that out, not just noticing the argument, is analysis. You already do it.

models.title: Where does chocolate come from?
lines: Rami finds out that chocolate is made from cocoa beans. Cocoa trees grow in hot, rainy places, especially in West Africa.
Farmers grow the pods, dry the beans, and sell them. The beans travel far away by ship to big factories, and come back as chocolate bars in the shop.

Then Rami finds a problem. The farmers who grow the cocoa are often paid very little, even though chocolate sells for a lot in shops far away. Sometimes children have to work on the farms instead of going to school.
Fair trade is one answer: it means paying farmers a fairer price, so their families earn enough and their children can go to school.

This topic is close to home, too. The Horn of Africa also grows and sells goods to the world, like bananas, sesame seeds and frankincense, which travel out through Berbera port. Farmers here can join a cooperative, which is a group of farmers who work together so they can be paid a fairer price. So Rami's question, who grows it and who gets paid fairly, matters in his own region too.

models.title: The kite competition
lines: Rami's class held a competition to make the best kite. Yusuf had bright paper, smooth sticks, string and glue. Malik had only an old newspaper and no glue at all.
Yusuf made a beautiful kite and won. Malik's kite fell apart.
Yusuf's perspective: the competition was fair, because everyone had to make a kite and mine was the best.
Malik's perspective: the competition was unfair, because we did not all start with the same materials, so I never had an equal chance.
Both give a reason. And notice the big idea: the competition was unequal, because the children had different materials, and that made it unfair.

models.title: The tower-building challenge
lines: Rami's class did a tower-building challenge in four groups. Each group had four children, but a different number of building pieces. They wrote the results in a table.
Blue group: 20 pieces, and they scored 9 points.
Red group: 15 pieces, and they scored 6 points.
Green group: 10 pieces, and they scored 7 points.
Yellow group: 5 pieces, and they scored 3 points.
Nadia looked at the table and said: the more pieces you have, the higher your score.

Was Nadia right? The data mostly backs her up. The group with the most pieces (Blue) did score the highest, and the group with the fewest (Yellow) scored the lowest. But look carefully: Green, with only 10 pieces, beat Red, who had 15. So Nadia is mostly right, not completely right. Checking a claim against the data, instead of just believing it, is real analysis.

models.title: Rami thinks about how he helps
lines: In my home: I helped my little brother learn his letters, and I made it into a game, because he is small and it is hard for him.
In my neighbourhood: I helped pick up litter in the town park with my neighbours, because everyone should be able to enjoy a clean park.
For a wider community: our class held a small sale and gave the money to help children who cannot afford school books, because every child deserves to learn.
Each action has a reason, and each one affects other people in a good way.

Once you can name your own helpful actions, you can start to spot local topics that need help. A local topic is a small problem right where you live. Here are some real ones Year 4 children have noticed:

models.title: Reading the town's fresh-food data
lines: District 6 had the most fresh-food shops, with 5. District 4 had none at all.
District 3 had the most older people. District 4 had the most families who were poor.
Idris looked at the table and said: I think most older people live in Districts 3 and 4.
Rami checked. Districts 3 and 4 did have the most older people, so the data showed Idris was right.
Then Amara said something important: the poorer a district is, the fewer fresh-food shops it has, and that is not fair.

When Rami checked Amara's claim against the table, he found a clear pattern: the districts with the most poor families really did have the fewest fresh-food shops. The data backed her up. Whether it is not fair is a perspective, and a perspective needs reasons. But a good analyst first checks: does the data support the claim, yes or no?

models.title: Rami plans to visit the elders
lines: Where: at the place near the market where the older people of the neighbourhood like to sit together.
What: Rami and two friends will visit, bring some fresh fruit, sit with the elders and listen to their stories.
Why: elders are respected in our community, and some of them do not get many visitors and can feel lonely.
What he found out first: he asked a neighbour, who said the elders would love some young company.
How it affects others: the elders feel happy, remembered and cheered. How it affects Rami: he feels proud, and he learns from their stories.
What difference it makes: young and old spend time together, and nobody is left out.

Notice how Rami thought about the elders' feelings, not only his own idea. That is what makes an action kind and well planned. Visiting and cheering our elders is a lovely example, because caring for older people is important in our community.

models.title: Why people feel differently about the park fee
lines: A child says the park should be free, because it is the only place with space to run, and not every family can pay.
A grandmother is not worried about the fee, because people over 65 get in free anyway.
A parent with several children worries, because a small fee for each child adds up to a lot.
The park keeper wants some fee, because the money keeps the grass cut and the park safe.
Each perspective makes sense once you know the reason behind it.

See how the same fee looks cheap to one person and dear to another? That is not because anyone is being silly. It is because the fee affects each of them differently. Explaining that reason is the skill.

models.title: What the park visitor data shows
lines: The most children came in August, straight after the new water-play fountain opened. That was almost certainly why.
The fewest children came in July, when it was very hot and the fountain had not opened yet.
Adult visitors dropped the most in May. That is when the fee went up, so it is likely the fee put some adults off.
The number of elders stayed almost the same all along, because elders get in free, so the higher fee did not change their visits.

Look how each conclusion links a number to a reason: more children came because of the new fountain; fewer adults came because of the fee. That is using data to reach a conclusion. Be careful, though: only say what the data really shows. The data does not tell us whether people enjoyed the park, only how many came.

models.title: Two very different reactions
lines: Mr Silva pays taxes but never uses the park. He is glad it might close, because he thinks it is unfair to pay for a park he never visits. His action: he writes to the council to sell the land.
Maya plays in the park every day. She is very sad, because it is her only place to play and see friends. Her action: she joins a campaign to save the park.
Same news, two feelings, because the park affects the two of them in different ways.

Soon a bright poster appeared on the noticeboard: Save Our Park! People could take different actions to help: make posters to spread the word, write a letter with many names to ask the council to listen, volunteer to tidy the park, or hold a fun day to raise money. A good analyst weighs each action and asks: which one would be the most effective? You choose the action most likely to actually save the park.

models.title: Rami's whole journey
lines: Rami started by saying what one person thought, with a reason, and learned the difference between equal and fair.
He read data in tables, and checked whether claims about towers, towns and countries were really true.
He saw that many people think different things about chocolate, a park and fresh food, and he explained why.
He planned a kind action to cheer the elders, and helped choose the most effective way to save the park.
Step by step, Rami turned a simple wonder about chocolate into clear, fair thinking.
You will do the very same thing with your own Challenge, one small step at a time, with your AI tutor beside you the whole way.

models.title: A model, in case you get stuck
lines: Topic: the town park needs a tidy-up.
The problem: there is litter on the grass, so it is not nice to play there.
My action: I could join a Saturday litter-pick with my neighbours, and bring a bag and gloves.
It is a small action, but it makes a real difference for everyone who uses the park.

models.title: Rami's plan, to help you
lines: Where: the place near the market where the elders like to sit.
What: visit with two friends, bring fresh fruit, and listen to their stories.
Why: elders are respected, and some can feel lonely.
How it affects others: the elders feel cheered. How it affects Rami: he feels proud and learns from them.

models.title: A model, to help you
lines: Mr Silva pays taxes but never uses the park. Happy or sad: glad. Reason: he thinks it is unfair to pay for a park he never uses. Action: he writes to the council to sell the land.
Maya plays there every day. Happy or sad: very sad. Reason: it is her only place to play and see friends. Action: she joins a campaign to save the park.
Same news, but two different feelings, because the park affects them differently.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Say hello to your AI tutor. Tell it: I am starting Unit 2 of Global Perspectives, and the skill is Analysis.
Ask it: in one or two simple sentences, what is the difference between finding out about something and analysing it?
Then tell it one topic near you that you would like to understand better, and why it matters to you.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor, in your own words, what you think analysis means now.
Ask it: how is analysing a topic different from just finding out about it?
Then tell it a small everyday moment, like two friends who want different games, and ask it to help you find one reason and one way it affects other people.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor about a time something felt unfair to you.
Ask it to help you say your perspective in one sentence, using the word because.
Then ask the tutor: what is the difference between something being equal and something being fair?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor about the tower table above.
Ask it to help you say, in one sentence, what the data shows.
Then ask: is Nadia completely right, mostly right, or not right at all, and how can you tell from the numbers?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor one local topic near you that could be better.
Ask it to help you say what the problem is in one clear sentence.
Then ask the tutor to help you think of one small action you could take to help.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your Challenge topic in one sentence.
Ask it to help you think of three different people who would see it in three different ways.
Then ask the tutor to argue one of those perspectives, so you can hear a view that is not your own.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor about the town where poorer districts had fewer fresh-food shops.
Ask it: is that a fact the data shows, or is it just an opinion?
Then ask the tutor whether you agree that this is not fair, and to help you say your reason.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor one action you could take to help someone near you.
Ask it to help you plan it: where, what, why, and how it affects other people.
Then ask the tutor: how will I know my action really helped?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor about the park fee, and how a child, a parent and a grandmother might each feel.
Ask it to help you explain why each one feels the way they do.
Then ask the tutor: on my own Challenge topic, why might two people think very differently?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor about the park visitor data and the two notes: the fee rise and the new fountain.
Ask it to help you write one conclusion that links a number to a reason.
Then ask the tutor: is there anything I am saying that the data does not really prove?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor about the two people who reacted differently to the park news.
Ask it to help you explain why the same news made them feel such different things.
Then ask the tutor to help you choose which Save Our Park action might be the most effective, and why.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your topic and your reason.
Ask it: is this a good topic for analysis, or do people mostly already agree about it?
Ask the tutor to suggest one person whose perspective on my topic I might easily forget.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your two perspectives to your AI tutor and ask if each one has a clear reason.
Ask it whether you have shown the difference between equal and fair.
Then ask the tutor to help you cheer Malik up with one idea for making the next competition fair.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your five answers to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether you described the pattern clearly, and whether you spotted the group that does not fit.
Ask the tutor how you could show this data as a bar chart, and what the tallest and shortest bars would be.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your local topic and your idea for an action.
Ask it: is my action something a Year 4 child could really do?

toolkit.title: What is analysis?
toolkit.intro:
Analysis means looking closely at a topic to understand the parts inside it. Instead of treating it as one big lump, you ask careful questions: What do different people think, and why? What does the data show? Why do things happen, and how do actions affect people? What is the best thing to do?

Two habits sit at the heart of it. First, always look for more than one perspective, because every topic looks different depending on who is looking. Second, always ask for the reason behind a view, or the data behind a claim, so you never treat an opinion as if it were a proven fact.

toolkit.title: The analysis steps at a glance
toolkit.intro: Whatever your topic, good analysis follows the same steps. Come back to this list whenever you feel lost.
items: See the perspectives, and ask each person for their reason.
Read the data in a chart or table, and say what it shows.
Check: does the data back up what someone said?
Think about actions: why people do things, and how they affect others.
Choose a positive action, and pick the most effective one.

toolkit.title: Your Stage 4 analysis learning goals
toolkit.intro: Your analysis skills grow in three steps this year. Here are your goals for each step, in simple words. It is fine to be working on any step.

toolkit.title: A frame for describing a perspective
toolkit.intro: A perspective is a way of seeing a topic. To describe one well, fill in this frame. The most important part is the reason.

rows: The person whose view this is.
Their point of view about the topic.
Why they think it. This is the key part.
The feeling behind the view, like happy or upset.

toolkit.title: Equal or fair? They are not the same
toolkit.intro:
These two words sound alike, but they mean different things. A good analyst keeps them apart.

Something can be equal but still feel unfair, like giving everyone the same materials when one child needs more help. Ask: did everyone really have a fair chance?

rows: Every child gets one pencil each.
Everyone gets what they need for a fair chance.
A child who lost their pencil is given one, so everyone can write.

toolkit.title: Causes and consequences
toolkit.intro: A cause is the reason why something happens. A consequence is what it leads to. Spotting both helps you understand a topic and think of a good action.

rows: A positive action that could help

toolkit.title: A frame for planning an action
toolkit.intro: When you want to help a local topic, plan your action first. This frame makes sure you think about other people, not only yourself.

rows: What did you find out first?
How will it affect other people?

toolkit.title: Choosing the most effective action
toolkit.intro: Often there is more than one thing you could do. The most effective action is the one that would work best. To choose, do not just pick the first idea. Weigh each one.
items: Would it really help the topic, or only look busy?
Can a child like me actually do it?
Who would it affect, and would anyone be worse off?
Which one, out of all of them, would make the biggest difference?

toolkit.title: Sentence starters for analysis
toolkit.intro: Use these to write clear analysis. Mix and match them as you need.

toolkit.title: For perspectives:
items: ... thinks that ... because ...
Another person might see it differently, because ...
One reason people disagree is ...

toolkit.title: For data:
items: The data shows that ...
The pattern I can see is ... For example ...
However, ... does not fit the pattern.
So my conclusion is ...

toolkit.title: For actions:
items: I did this because ...
This action would affect other people by ...
The most effective action would be ... because ...

checklists.title: Checklist: How to read the data
checklists.intro: When you meet a chart, table or graph, read it calmly in this order. It stops the numbers from fooling you.
items: Read the title. What is this data about?
Read the labels. What is being counted?
Find the biggest number and the smallest number.
Name the pattern. Do the numbers go up, go down, or stay the same?
Ask: does the data back up what someone claimed? Yes, mostly, or not at all?

activities.title: Fair or equal? Describe two perspectives
activities.label: Activity 2: Fair or equal? Describe two perspectives
activities.intro:
Remember the kite competition. Yusuf had bright paper, sticks, string and glue. Malik had only old newspaper and no glue. Yusuf made a fine kite and won. Malik's kite fell apart.

First, describe each boy's perspective. Use these sentence starters and word bank to help you.
steps: Write Yusuf's perspective in two sentences, with a reason.
Write Malik's perspective in two sentences, with a reason.
Was the competition equal? Was it fair? Explain the difference in your own words.
Rate it: was the competition completely fair, mostly fair, mostly unfair, or completely unfair? Give your reason.
How could you change the competition to make it fair for everyone next time?

boxes.title: Sentence starters and word bank
lines: Sentence starters: ... thinks the competition was ... This is because ... He feels ...
Word bank: happy, upset, fair, unfair, equal, unequal, deserved, did not deserve, materials, chance.
Every perspective needs the word because, followed by a reason.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor

Ask it whether you have shown the difference between equal and fair.
Then ask the tutor to help you cheer Malik up with one idea for making the next competition fair.

activities.title: Read the data and test a claim
activities.label: Activity 3: Read the data and test a claim
activities.intro: Analysts must be able to read data, not just collect it. The table below shows the tower-building challenge. Each group had four children, but a different number of building pieces. Read it carefully, then answer the questions.
steps: Which group had the most building pieces? Which had the fewest?
Which group scored the highest? Which scored the lowest?
Nadia says: 'The more pieces you have, the higher your score.' Look at Green and Red. Does the data completely back her up?
Write one sentence saying what the data shows: is Nadia completely right, mostly right, or not right at all?
Was it fair to give the groups different numbers of pieces? Give your reason.

activities.label: Activity 4: Spot a local topic and plan a first action
activities.intro: Analysis leads to action. First, think about how you already help at home, in your neighbourhood, and for a wider community. Then find a local topic you could help with.
steps: Write one helpful thing you have done at home, in your neighbourhood, or for a wider community. Say what you did and why.
Now look at the local topics from the Lesson: the town park, internet for homework, fresh fruit and vegetables, a computer club, the community garden. Choose one that matters near you.
Write in one sentence what the problem is.
Write one small action you could take to help.

My action: I could join a Saturday litter-pick with my neighbours, and bring a bag and gloves.
It is a small action, but it makes a real difference for everyone who uses the park.

activities.label: Activity 5: Find the useful data to answer a question
activities.intro: The table below shows six districts of a town. For each district it shows the number of fresh fruit and vegetable shops, how many people in every 100 are older (over 65), and how many families in every 100 are poor. Read it carefully, then answer the questions.
steps: Which district has the most fresh-food shops? Which has none at all?
Which district has the most older people? Which has the most poorer families?
Idris says: 'Most older people live in Districts 3 and 4.' Look at the table. Is he right? How do you know?
Amara says: 'The poorer a district is, the fewer fresh-food shops it has.' Is this true in the data? Give an example from the table.
Amara also says this is 'not fair'. Do you agree? Give your reason. (Remember: whether it is fair is a perspective.)

activities.title: Plan an action to cheer someone
activities.label: Activity 6: Plan an action to cheer someone
activities.intro:
Now plan a real action, thinking about how it affects other people, not just yourself. Rami planned to visit the elders. You can plan the same kind of action, or a different one that helps someone near you.

Copy the table below and fill in each row for your own action.

rows: What did you find out first?
How will it affect other people?

boxes.title: Rami's plan, to help you
lines: Where: the place near the market where the elders like to sit.
What: visit with two friends, bring fresh fruit, and listen to their stories.
Why: elders are respected, and some can feel lonely.
How it affects others: the elders feel cheered. How it affects Rami: he feels proud and learns from them.

activities.title: Compare with data, and find the odd one out
activities.label: Activity 7: Compare with data, and find the odd one out
activities.intro: The table below shows five made-up countries. For each one it shows how much money each person makes in a year, and how many doctors there are for every 1,000 people. Read it, then answer the questions.
steps: Which country has the most money per person? Which has the least?
Which country has the most doctors for every 1,000 people? Which has the fewest?
Idris says: 'Usually, the richer a country is, the more doctors it has.' Is this mostly true in the data? Give two examples.
One country is a surprise: it is rich, but it has very few doctors. Which country breaks the pattern?
If you had to live in one of these countries, which would you choose, and why? What other information would help you decide?

activities.title: Read data over time and reach a conclusion
activities.label: Activity 8: Read data over time and reach a conclusion
activities.intro: The table below shows how many visitors came to the Green Park each week, month by month. Two things happened during the year: the entrance fee went up on the first of May, and a new water-play fountain opened at the end of July. Children pay half price, and elders over 65 get in free. June and July were very hot.
steps: Which month had the most child visitors? What probably caused that?
Which month had the fewest child visitors? Why might that be?
Adult visitors dropped the most between April and May. What probably caused that?
The number of elders stayed about the same all year. Why do you think the fee rise did not change it?
Was raising the fee a good decision? Give one reason for, and one reason against.

activities.title: Two people, two different reactions
activities.label: Activity 9: Two people, two different reactions
activities.intro: A headline says the Green Park might close, because it costs the town a lot of money each year. People react differently, because the park affects them in different ways. Imagine two people and fill in the table.
steps: Think of two people the park closing would affect in different ways.
Fill in the table for both: are they happy or sad, what is their reason, and what action do they take?
Write one sentence explaining why the same news made your two people feel such different things.

boxes.title: A model, to help you
lines: Mr Silva pays taxes but never uses the park. Happy or sad: glad. Reason: he thinks it is unfair to pay for a park he never uses. Action: he writes to the council to sell the land.
Maya plays there every day. Happy or sad: very sad. Reason: it is her only place to play and see friends. Action: she joins a campaign to save the park.
Same news, but two different feelings, because the park affects them differently.

activities.title: Choose the most effective action
activities.label: Activity 10: Choose the most effective action
activities.intro:
A poster appears: Save Our Park! People could take different actions to try to save it. Your job is to weigh them and choose the one that would work best.

Here are four possible actions. Think about how well each one would work, and how it would affect other people.
steps: Make posters and tell people, so more of the town knows the park is in danger.
Write a letter with many names on it, asking the council to listen.
Volunteer to tidy the park, so it looks cared for and loved.
Hold a fun day to raise money to help keep the park open.
For each action, write one good thing about it.
Choose the action you think would be the most effective, and give your reason.
Now plan it. Copy this table and fill it in: Our action / Who will be involved / What we hope to achieve.

practice.intro: Answer these in your notebook or out loud with your AI tutor. There are 14 questions. Do not worry if some are tricky; that is how you find out what to practise next. Use your own words.
practice.prompt: In your own words, what does the word 'analysis' mean?
practice.answer: Analysis means looking closely at a topic to understand it: the different ways people think, what the data shows, why things happen, and what could be done. (Any answer with this idea is correct.)

practice.prompt: A way of seeing a topic, a point of view, is called a ______.
practice.answer: A perspective.

practice.prompt: What is the difference between being equal and being fair?
practice.answer: Equal means everyone gets exactly the same. Fair means everyone gets what they need for a fair chance. They are not always the same.

practice.prompt: True or false: a good perspective just says what you think, with no reason.
practice.answer: False. A good perspective gives a reason, usually with the word because.

practice.prompt: When you read a chart or table, what should you look at first?
practice.answer: The title (what it is about), then the labels, then the numbers.

practice.prompt: Something the data does again and again, like numbers going up in order, is called a ______.
practice.answer: A pattern.

practice.prompt: True or false: 'Chocolate tastes nicer than fruit' is a fact.
practice.answer: False. It is an opinion, because other people might disagree; it cannot be checked.

practice.prompt: A ______ is the reason why something happens; a ______ is what it leads to.
practice.answer: A cause is the reason why something happens; a consequence is what it leads to.

practice.prompt: The effect an action has on people is called its ______.
practice.answer: Its impact.

practice.prompt: Why is it useful to look at data when you analyse a topic?
practice.answer: Because data can show what is really happening, and can check whether an opinion is actually true.

practice.prompt: When someone takes an action, a good analyst asks: how does it ______ other people?
practice.answer: Affect.

practice.prompt: What does fair trade try to do for the farmers who grow cocoa?
practice.answer: It tries to pay the farmers a fairer price, so their families earn enough and their children can go to school.

practice.prompt: When you choose between different actions, you pick the one that is most ______.
practice.answer: Effective.

practice.prompt: Name one positive action a child could take to help a local topic.
practice.answer: Any sensible action, such as: pick up litter, join a campaign, help in the community garden, tell people, or choose fair-trade chocolate.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.intro: Match each analysis word (1 to 8) to the right meaning (A to H). Write the pairs, like 1-C.
practice.prompt: Perspective
options: A. The reason why something happens.
B. A way of seeing a topic; a point of view.
C. Something that can be checked and shown to be true.
D. The effect an action has on people.
E. Something the data does again and again, like numbers rising in order.
F. What something leads to; the result.
G. Information in numbers, like counts in a chart or table.
H. What someone thinks or feels, which others may not agree with.
practice.answer: B — A way of seeing a topic; a point of view.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning

practice.answer: C — Something that can be checked and shown to be true.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Opinion

practice.prompt: Cause
practice.answer: A — The reason why something happens.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Consequence
practice.answer: F — What something leads to; the result.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Data
practice.answer: G — Information in numbers, like counts in a chart or table.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Impact
practice.answer: D — The effect an action has on people.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning

practice.answer: E — Something the data does again and again, like numbers rising in order.

practice.intro: These short questions ask you to use what you learned. Write a sentence or two for each.
practice.prompt: Yusuf won the kite competition because he had the best materials, while Malik had almost none. Was the competition equal? Was it fair? Explain.
practice.answer: It was unequal, because the boys had different materials, and so it was unfair, because they did not have the same chance to win.

practice.prompt: Nadia says 'the more pieces, the higher the score.' The data shows Blue (most pieces) scored highest and Yellow (fewest) scored lowest, but Green beat Red with fewer pieces. Is Nadia completely right?
practice.answer: She is mostly right, not completely right. More pieces mostly meant more points, but Green beat Red with fewer pieces, so the data does not completely back her up.

practice.prompt: Amara says poorer districts have fewer fresh-food shops, and that is not fair. Which part is a fact the data shows, and which part is a perspective?
practice.answer: That poorer districts have fewer fresh-food shops is a fact the data shows. That it is 'not fair' is a perspective, which needs a reason.

practice.prompt: In the country data, Petrania is rich but has very few doctors. What do we call a country that breaks the pattern like this?
practice.answer: An outlier, or a country that breaks the pattern.

practice.prompt: Rami plans to visit the elders and listen to their stories. Give one reason for his action, and say how it affects other people.
practice.answer: Reason: elders are respected and some can feel lonely. Effect: it cheers the elders and makes them feel remembered, and Rami feels proud and learns from them.

practice.prompt: The park may close. Mr Silva is glad, but Maya is sad. Why do two people feel so differently about the same news?
practice.answer: Because the park affects them differently. Maya plays there and would lose her only place to play, while Mr Silva pays taxes but never uses it. Different perspectives come from how the topic affects each person.

Choosing the first action, without weighing the others.
Forgetting to ask how an action affects other people.
